name: Frequency Illusion
description: After noticing something once, people can feel as if it suddenly appears everywhere. The experience is usually described as a mix of selective noticing and biased interpretation of subsequent encounters rather than a settled standalone experimental law.
design_relevance_note: Mostly relevant as a caution in user research, trend spotting, and analytics interpretation: once a team notices a pattern, it can start overestimating how common the pattern really is. This is not a strong direct interface-design mechanism in the way anchoring or banner blindness are.
myth_risk_note: Updated 2026-09-07: myth risk stays moderate. Real backing now exists for a frequency-estimation mechanism in this space, but the specific, most commonly invoked version of this bias in casual usage (the Baader-Meinhof 'notice it once, see it everywhere' framing) still has no direct peer-reviewed test.
prevalence_note: Internet-famous and occasionally mentioned in research/strategy conversations, but not part of the core named UX canon and not commonly used as a formal design rationale.

findings.description: Splitting an event category into smaller subcategories systematically inflates people's subjective estimate of how frequent those events are, via an information-loss-in-memory mechanism -- demonstrated across 3 experiments, including one showing the effect can produce illusory group-related correlations. This is a real, replicated frequency-estimation bias, but it is a distinct mechanism from the popular 'Baader-Meinhof phenomenon' framing of this BiasHeuristic (suddenly noticing something everywhere right after first learning of it) -- this study never manipulates or measures a noticing-triggered salience effect at all.
findings.effect_size: Regressive frequency-estimate bias reobtained across 3 experiments; no single pooled effect size reported
findings.source_title: Two halfs may be more than one whole: Category-split effects on frequency illusions
findings.source_venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
